Short · ~45 words

Gestalt Lite is a free, self-guided audio walk of eleven Philadelphia murals. Visitors open the trail map in their phone's browser and hear each wall's story aloud — in English or Spanish, with no app, no signup, and no cost. Live at gestalt.gallery.

Long · ~95 words

Gestalt Lite turns Philadelphia's most famous walls into a free audio walking trail. Eleven murals — including Amy Sherald's six-story portrait on Sansom Street, Keith Haring's We The Youth, and Meg Saligman's Common Threads — each plays the story of its wall aloud from a free browser map, in English or Spanish. The experience runs entirely in the browser: no app, no account, no trackers, and it meets WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards. Gestalt Lite was designed and built in Philadelphia by Gestalt, which makes audio-first accessibility infrastructure for museums and public art.

The story

A mural says everything to the people who made it, and nothing to the person walking past.

Stand in front of one of Philadelphia's great murals and there's no guide, no app worth downloading, no plaque deep enough. The history, the artist, the reason it's six stories tall: all of it stays on the wall.

Gestalt Lite changes that with the lightest possible technology. A free map in the phone's browser, one tap, and the story is playing aloud. The pilot trail of eleven murals launched in June 2026, as hundreds of thousands of international visitors arrive in Philadelphia for the summer's matches — many of them Spanish speakers, all of them with hours to fill between kickoffs, and every one of them carrying the only device the trail needs.

Story angles

The free hour between matches

Half a million visitors, one trail that costs nothing and starts wherever they're standing. Common Threads sits at Broad & Spring Garden, directly on the walk between Fairmount Park and Center City.

The city, en español

Every stop plays in Spanish as well as English — built for the international visitors arriving this summer and for Philadelphia's Spanish-speaking residents year-round.

Public art, finally accessible

Audio-first and WCAG 2.1 AA throughout: the trail makes the city's most famous visual art available to blind and low-vision visitors during the biggest tourism event in Philadelphia's history.

Built in Philadelphia, in a browser

A solo Philly founder's bet that cities need an audio layer the way websites needed mobile — shipped web-first, with audio playing moments after the map opens and no app store in the way.

Founder

Chris Carter, Founder & CEO

Chris Carter is a Philadelphia-based experience designer and design technologist with more than fourteen years in innovation, including design engineering at Capital One and service design for Con Edison's field operations. He founded Gestalt to build audio-first accessibility infrastructure for museums, galleries, and public art — starting with the city he lives in. Gestalt Lite, the company's web-first product, narrates a collection and generates its scannable codes within days of receiving an artwork list.

Chris is available for interviews, on-camera walks of the trail, and live demos. (Headshot available on request.)

Quick answers
Is it really free?
Yes — for everyone, indefinitely. Nothing on the trail is gated, and there's no account or signup.
What do visitors actually do?
Open mural.gestalt.gallery/nearby in the phone's browser. The map shows the closest of the eleven murals, audio plays in one tap, and the next wall and the walking distance to reach it follow.
How does Gestalt make money?
Gestalt Lite is the public face of a product for cities and cultural institutions: send an artwork list, and Gestalt narrates the collection, generates the codes, and reports real engagement — plays, time-to-audio, and how many people walked to a second work.
What's next?
More walls and more cities. Philadelphia is the first walk; the same accessible audio layer can cover a gallery, a sculpture garden, or an entire city's public art.
